I have worked this land for forty years. I know every uneven patch of my 10.1 mu. My husband and I are the only ones left in the house — our children went to the city — so I must be careful with labor and money. We have a well, but pumping water costs electricity, and I do not waste a single kilowatt.

For wheat, I will sow improved seeds from the supply store in town, the kind my neighbors also plant. I prepare the field with rotary tillage before October sowing. I put down compound fertilizer as a base and top-dress with urea in spring when the wheat turns green and again at jointing — about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu in total. I also apply about 8 kg of phosphorus and 5 kg of potassium per mu with the basal fertilizer. I irrigate three times: once before winter freeze to protect the roots, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I spray pesticides three times — herbicide in early spring, then insecticide and fungicide when the weather turns warm. If frost and drought stay away, I expect about 500 kg per mu.

For summer maize, the window after wheat harvest in early June is short — only six or seven days. I plant hybrid maize seed right away using no-tillage; there is no time to plow, and at my age I need to save labor. Maize needs more nitrogen than wheat, so I apply about 18 kg per mu — compound fertilizer at sowing and urea at the big trumpet stage. I put down about 6 kg of phosphorus and 5 kg of potassium per mu with the basal compound fertilizer. The summer rains usually help, but I will irrigate twice if they fail, at jointing and filling. I spray three times: herbicide, insecticide for corn borer, and a growth regulator. I expect about 550 kg per mu.
